The Navajo
History

The Navajo people (or Diné), like the Apaches, are of Athapaskan descent and probably migrated south to the American Southwest about 1300, although archaeological evidence suggests that some Athapaskan-speaking tribes arrived in the Four Corners region of Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Utah as early as the 8th century. Oral tradition holds that the ancestors of the Navahos were already in Dinétah (the traditional Navaho homeland) when the Anasazi were building in Chaco Canyon between the years 900 and 1130. The Navaho conflicts that led up to the Long Walk began with the Spanish conquest of the Southwest in the 16th century. Before the Conquistadors arrived, the early Navahos apparently coexisted with their Pueblo Indian neighbors fairly well, though raids were sometimes carried out. The Navahos, seminomadic hunters, adopted some Pueblo culture and learned farming from the Pueblo tribes. Spanish missionaries had almost no success with the Navahos, but the Navahos did take an interest in Spanish horses and guns and, as a result, their interest in raiding grew. Sometimes the Navahos raided the Spanish colonists, and sometimes they traded with them. But they were far enough away not to feel too threatened by the Spaniards. The Pueblo Indians had it worse. Spanish soldiers and priests were living among them, forcing the Indians to forego their traditions and to worship the Spanish God. To seek refuge from their heavy-handed masters, some Pueblos ran off to join the Navahos. In 1680, the Pueblo people revolted against their Spanish masters and drove them away from New Mexico, but all their problems did not disappear with the Spaniards. The Navahos, mounted on horses, increasingly raided Pueblo villages. In some cases, Spanish soldiers had been providing protection from these raids. Not that the Pueblo Indians wanted the white men to return, but return they did in 1692. When the Spanish reconquered New Mexico, many Pueblos again fled to live with friendly Navaho bands. This cultural mix led to the Navahos’ learning many new things, including how to raise sheep and goats. In time, as the Spaniards took a kinder approach to the Pueblo Indians, many of the Pueblo families that had taken up residence in Dinétah returned to their pueblo homes. By the early 1700s, most Pueblos were siding with the Spaniards, who could help fight off Navaho, Apache and Ute raiders. At the same time, the Spanish, sometimes with Pueblo assistance, were busy capturing Navaho women, children and livestock.By the end of the 18th century, the Navahos were also dealing with equally troubling raids by Utes, Comanches, Jicarilla Apaches and Mescalero Apaches. Many Navahos packed up and drove their flocks to more peaceful grazing grounds to the west.
Manuelito

Greetings, brave chief Hastiin Chʼil Haajiní, strenous defender of the Navajo people against the white invaders, who knew you under the name of Manuelito. Determined to become a war leader, you fought your first battle at Narbona Pass in 1835 when 1000 Mexicans were coming to attack the Navajo, earning the nickname Hashkeh Naabaah,″Angry Warrior″. Having become the principal chief of the Navajo in 1855, you resisted the offenses of the US Army until the General James Carleton ordered a scorched-earth campain against your people in 1861. Starved and exhausted, thousand Navajos surrendered turning themselves into Fort Defiance, whence the infamous forced relocation to the Bosque Redondo reservation known as Long Walk started in 1864. Your people endured miserable and inhumane living conditions until June 1st, 1868, when you and other leaders signed a treaty that allowed your people to return home and recognized the Navajo as a sovereign nation.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Valiant chief Manuelito, the Navajo people needs you once again. Will you answer their call and fearlessly guide them in peace and war? Will you build a civilization that stands the test of time?
History

Manuelito (1818–1893) was one of the principal war chiefs of the Diné people before, during and after the Long Walk Period. His name means Little Manuel in Spanish. He was born to the Bit'aa'nii or Folded Arms People Clan, near the Bear's Ears in southeastern Utah about 1818. As any Navajo, he was known by different names depending upon context. He was Ashkii Diyinii (Holy Boy), Dahaana Baadaané (Son-in-Law of Late Texan), Hastiin Ch'ilhaajiní ("Black Weeds") and as Nabááh Jitt'aa (War Chief, "Warrior Grabbed Enemy") to other Diné, and non-Navajo nicknamed him "Bullet Hole".

[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]A hogan is the traditional dwelling of the Navajo Indians of Arizona and New Mexico used also for religious ceremonials. Early hogans were dome-shaped buildings with log, or occasionally stone, frameworks. Once framed, the structure was then covered with mud, dirt, or sometimes sod. The entrance generally faced east, toward the rising sun, and was usually covered with a blanket. Except for a circular opening in the roof to allow smoke to escape, traditional hogans were without windows or interior divisions. [NEWLINE]By the early 21st century, hogan architecture had changed somewhat to accommodate new construction materials and techniques. Typically hexagonal or octagonal buildings with notched-log or balloon-frame construction, they maintained traditional design elements such as the generally circular floor plan and eastward-facing door.

The Navajo term hataalii, also spelled yataalii, translates as into English as "singer". Singers are medicine men who perform traditional healing ceremonies and blessing rites intended to protect and cure the body, mind, and spirit. Singers use traditional, sacred practices such as chanting, praying, or herb medicine to call on the ill person, his kin, the singer himself, and divine beings to restore the individual's health in accordance with communal balance and universal harmony. Healing or blessing rituals vary according to the occasion, but singing is the main component in all of them, and there are hundreds of songs that comprise a variety of chants. [NEWLINE]There are nearly 100 Navajo chants, originating in Navajo origin mythology, and varying in range and intricacy. They are so nuanced and complex that a singer learns only one or two complete chants over many years of apprenticeship. Healing ceremonies last anywhere from one to nine days and include songs, prayers, talks, dances, sweat baths, and sand paintings.

Code talker, any of more than 400 Native American soldiers —including Assiniboin, Cherokee, Cheyenne, Choctaw, Comanche, Cree, Crow, Fox, Hopi, Kiowa, Menominee, Navajo, Ojibwa, Oneida, Osage, Pawnee, Sauk, Seminole, and Sioux men— who transmitted sensitive wartime messages by speaking their native languages, in effect using them as codes. In both World War I and World War II, but especially the latter, the code talkers provided U.S. forces with fast communications over open radio waves, knowing that the enemy was unable to break the code. By all accounts the service of the code talkers was crucial to winning World War II in the Pacific theatre.

Diyogí is the Navajo name for rug or blanket. According to Navajo tradition, they were taught to weave by two holy ones: Spider Man and Spider Woman. The legend says that Spider Man created the loom of sunshine, lightning and rain, while Spider Woman taught the Navajo how to weave it.[NEWLINE]Historically, they picked up the skill of weaving sometime in the 17th century. Although scholars speculate that the Navajo picked up the skill from the neighboring Pueblo tribe, the Navajo people eventually came to be recognized as the most skillful of all the Native American weavers, dexterously crafting pieces prized for their vivid patterns, durability and all-around practicality.[NEWLINE]Traditional blankets were simple in design— early Pueblo blankets prominently featured banded stripe-patterns. The main colors of early blankets were typically grey, brown, tan, white or black, which was due to the natural color of the Churro sheep. Stripes were also colored with indigo, which could be obtained from indigofera shrubs imported from Mexico on pony caravans. The Navajo favored the color red, as it’s frequent in their weaving, but it was difficult to obtain red vegetable dyes in the Southwest. [NEWLINE]Navajo rugs are highly abstract; designs convey ideas through symbols and lines, as well as colors. Skilled weavers know the different styles based upon regional designs, and can create unique rugs that stay true to the original ideas. [NEWLINE]A 1973 study conducted with Dine Community College has estimated that it takes an average of 344 hours, or over two weeks of active time, to make a blanket: 45 hours to sheer the sheep, 24 hours to spin the wool, 60 hours to prep and dye wool, and 215 hours to weave.

At'looh is a Navajo verb describing the act of weaving textiles. [NEWLINE]Introduced to weaving by the Pueblo people in the 17th century, the Navajo quickly developed their own unique style, distinguished by complex geometric patterns, vibrant colors, and the use of natural materials such as wool from their sheep. Each piece, often crafted by hand on an upright loom, carries cultural significance and stories, reflecting the weaver's personal expressions and the broader Navajo cosmology. Renowned for their beauty and craftsmanship, Navajo rugs and blankets have become highly collectible and are celebrated for their artistry and cultural heritage.

Naabaahii means 'warrior' or 'raider' in Navajo. [NEWLINE]Navajo raiding tactics were a critical aspect of their survival and resistance strategies in the harsh environment of the American Southwest. These tactics were honed over centuries and involved highly organized and stealthy operations. Navajo raiders would typically target livestock, supplies, and other resources from neighboring tribes and later from Spanish, Mexican, and American settlers. The raiders relied on their intimate knowledge of the rugged terrain, using it to their advantage to approach their targets undetected and escape swiftly. The element of surprise was crucial, and raids were meticulously planned to avoid direct confrontation whenever possible, minimizing casualties on both sides. They often conducted raids during the night or early dawn to exploit the cover of darkness, enhancing their stealth and effectiveness. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The raids were not merely acts of aggression but were deeply intertwined with Navajo economic, social, and cultural systems. Livestock obtained from raids bolstered the Navajo economy, supporting their pastoral lifestyle and increasing their wealth and status within the community. The skills and bravery demonstrated in successful raids were highly valued, enhancing the reputation of the raiders. Moreover, these tactics were a form of resistance against encroaching colonial powers, serving as a means to assert Navajo autonomy and disrupt the expansion of settlers into their territories. This guerrilla warfare approach, combining traditional knowledge with adaptive strategies, underscored the resilience and adaptability of the Navajo people in the face of external pressures and changing circumstances.

나바호인(또는 디네족)은 아파치족과 마찬가지로 아타파스칸 계통의 후손으로, 약 1300년경 북쪽에서 아메리카 남서부로 이주한 것으로 추정된다. 고고학적 증거에 따르면 아타파스칸어를 사용하는 일부 부족은 이미 8세기경 애리조나, 뉴멕시코, 콜로라도, 유타가 만나는 포코너스 지역에 도착했다. 구전 전승에 따르면 나바호 조상들은 이미 디네타(전통적인 나바호의 고향)에 거주하며 900~1130년 사이 아나사지가 차코 캐니언에 건축물을 세울 때 존재했다. 16세기 스페인 정복 이후로 시작된 갈등은 결국 ‘긴 여정’으로 이어졌다. 초기 나바호들은 준유목 수렵민으로서 푸에블로 부족과 공존했으나, 때때로 습격도 벌였다. 이들은 푸에블로 문화 일부를 받아들이고 농사법도 배웠다. 스페인 선교사들은 나바호 개종에 거의 실패했지만, 나바호들은 말과 총에 흥미를 가져 점차 습격을 늘렸다. 그들은 스페인 식민자와 때로는 교역하고 때로는 공격했으나, 거리가 멀어 큰 위협은 느끼지 않았다. 반면 푸에블로인들은 직접적인 압박을 받았고, 일부는 나바호와 함께 살며 피신했다. 1680년 푸에블로 반란으로 스페인이 물러났지만, 문제는 완전히 사라지지 않았다. 나바호 기마부대는 푸에블로 마을을 자주 공격했고, 1692년 스페인이 재정복하자 다시 많은 푸에블로인들이 나바호와 동거하게 되었다. 이 문화적 교류로 나바호는 양과 염소를 기르는 법을 익혔다. 18세기 초가 되자 많은 푸에블로인들은 다시 스페인을 지지했고, 스페인과 푸에블로 동맹은 나바호·아파치·유트족에 맞섰다. 그 과정에서 스페인은 나바호 여성과 아이, 가축을 사로잡기도 했다. 18세기 말 나바호들은 유트, 코만치, 메스칼레로 아파치 등의 습격에도 시달렸고, 많은 이들이 서쪽의 평화로운 방목지로 옮겨가야 했다.
마누엘리토
용맹한 추장 하스틴 칠 하지니, 백인 침략자들에 맞서 나바호를 지켜낸 강인한 수호자여. 사람들은 당신을 마누엘리토라 불렀습니다. 전쟁 지도자가 되기를 결심한 당신은 1835년 나르보나 고개 전투에서 처음 싸웠으며, 이때 ‘화난 전사(하슈케 나아바)’라는 별명을 얻었습니다. 1855년 나바호의 최고 지도자가 된 이후, 당신은 미군의 공격에 맞서 싸웠습니다. 그러나 제임스 칼턴 장군이 1861년 초토화 작전을 명령하면서, 굶주리고 지친 수천 명의 나바호인들은 항복해 포트 디파이언스로 끌려갔습니다. 그곳에서 악명 높은 강제 이주, 보스케 레돈도 ‘긴 여정’이 1864년에 시작되었습니다. 당신의 백성은 비참하고 비인도적인 생활을 강요받았으나, 1868년 6월 1일 당신과 다른 지도자들이 조약에 서명하면서 고향으로 돌아올 수 있게 되었고, 나바호는 주권을 가진 민족으로 인정받았습니다.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]용맹한 마누엘리토 추장이여, 나바호 백성은 다시금 당신을 필요로 합니다. 그들의 부름에 응해 평화와 전쟁 속에서 두려움 없이 이끌어 주시겠습니까? 당신은 시간을 견뎌낼 문명을 세우시겠습니까?
역사
마누엘리토(1818–1893)는 ‘긴 여정’ 전후 나바호(디네)족의 주요 전쟁 지도자 중 한 명이었다. 그의 이름은 스페인어로 ‘작은 마누엘’을 뜻한다. 그는 1818년경 유타 남동부 베어스 이어즈 근처에서 ‘팔짱 낀 사람들 씨족’(비트아니) 출신으로 태어났다. 그는 상황에 따라 여러 이름으로 불렸다. 아시키 디이니(신성한 소년), 다하나 바다네(텍사스인의 사위), 하스틴 칠하지니(‘검은 잡초’), 나바 지트아(전사 추장, ‘적을 붙잡은 전사’) 등이다. 나바호 외부인들은 그를 ‘총알 구멍’이라는 별명으로 부르기도 했다.
